why: Just-in-time elevation grants privileges on request for a limited window and removes them afterwards, which eliminates standing privilege. Password length does not change what an account may do, recertification is periodic and leaves rights in place between reviews, and a second permanent privileged account is still standing privilege.

q: A SaaS application creates a user account the first time an employee signs in through the company identity provider. The employee later leaves, and the company disables the identity provider account. Which risk REMAINS if nothing else is done?
opts: The SaaS application will delete all other user accounts
The employee will automatically regain access through just-in-time provisioning
The local account in the SaaS application may persist unless deprovisioning is automated
The identity provider can no longer sign assertions for other employees
why: Just-in-time provisioning creates accounts but does not remove them, so a local account, tokens or API keys may live on without SCIM or similar deprovisioning. Disabling one user does not affect others, the application will not delete accounts on its own and a disabled identity cannot be provisioned again.

q: A company keeps Active Directory on premises and adopts a cloud identity service for its SaaS applications. Users should keep a single set of credentials and joiner, mover and leaver changes should apply to both. Which model is this?
opts: A discretionary access control design without central policy
A hybrid identity design with synchronization or federation between directory and cloud service
An air-gapped design with separate user lists in each environment, maintained by hand by two different administrative teams and never synchronized
A cloud-only design with the on-premises directory deleted
why: Keeping the on-premises directory while linking it to a cloud identity service is a hybrid model. Separate lists defeat the single-credential goal, deleting the directory contradicts keeping it and DAC describes who controls object permissions, not identity architecture.

q: In an access control architecture, the component that supplies attribute values, such as a user's department or a device's health, to the decision point is the:
opts: Policy information point
Policy decision point
Policy enforcement point
Policy administration point
why: The information point supplies the attributes that the decision point needs. The decision point evaluates the request, the enforcement point applies the decision at the resource and the administration point is where policies are authored.

q: A database view lets a manager see only the pay records for employees in their own department, and only during business hours. Which combination of ideas does this use?
opts: Mandatory access control with a lattice of clearances
Rule-based control only, with no regard for the data itself
Discretionary control where the data owner can share access at will, with no central policy about department membership or time of day
Content-dependent control (based on the data) with context-dependent control (based on time)
why: Filtering rows by their content and restricting time of day are, respectively, content-dependent and context-dependent controls. MAC compares clearances to labels, a purely rule-based model ignores content and DAC lets owners grant access freely.

q: During an annual access review, the reviewers are the system administrators who granted the access. An auditor objects. What is the BEST improvement?
opts: Reduce the review to once every five years to lessen effort
Ask users to review their own permissions and approve them
Have business or data owners attest to each user's access, with administrators only providing the data
Skip review of privileged accounts because they are already trusted, and focus the effort only on ordinary user accounts in business applications
why: Owners understand business need and are independent of the people who grant access. Skipping privileged accounts omits the highest risk, reviewing every five years is too infrequent and self-approval has no independence.

q: An audit finds a service account used by an integration job: it is a member of the domain administrators group, its password has not changed in six years and nobody knows who owns it. Which action is MOST important?
opts: Share the password with the whole operations team so that someone is always able to manage the account when the integration job fails at night
Rename the account so attackers cannot recognize it
Assign an owner, reduce its permissions to what the job needs, vault and rotate its secret and prevent interactive logon
Disable audit logging for the account because it creates noise
why: Ownership, least privilege, secret management and blocking interactive use remove the main risks. Disabling logging reduces detection, sharing the password destroys accountability and renaming is obscurity.

q: An identity provider outage locks every administrator out of the cloud console during an incident. The team wants a way in that works when single sign-on does not, without leaving a standing back door. Which design fits BEST?
opts: Turning off multi-factor authentication for all administrators for the duration of any outage
A break-glass account with a vaulted credential, alerts on every use, approval and a review afterwards
A shared administrator password written on a card kept in a locked drawer in the server room
Permanent local administrator accounts on every system, used by the whole team for daily work
why: Break-glass accounts are tightly controlled emergency accounts: the credential is vaulted or sealed, every use raises an alert and needs approval, and the use is reviewed and the credential rotated afterwards. A shared password on a card and permanent daily-use local accounts are standing exposures without accountability, and switching off MFA widens the attack surface exactly when the organization is under stress.

q: A Linux administrator needs to restart a service occasionally. The team currently shares the root password. Which design BEST follows least privilege and accountability?
opts: Grant that individual permission to run the restart command through sudo and log every use centrally
Give the administrator a permanent second account with unrestricted root rights, protected by a strong password stored in the team's shared password manager
Keep the shared root password but change it each year
Disable sudo and require physical console access for every action
why: Delegating only the needed command through sudo, with logging forwarded to a central system, gives named accountability and minimal rights. An unrestricted root account and a shared password are over-privileged, and banning sudo is impractical and does not give per-person audit.

q: Passwordless authentication with a passkey means that only one authentication factor is used, because there is no password.
opts: True
False
why: A passkey is a key held by the device (something you have) that is usually unlocked by a biometric or PIN (something you are or know), so it typically provides multiple factors in one gesture.

q: If a web application does not change the session identifier at login, an attacker who already knows the pre-login identifier may be able to use the authenticated session.
opts: True
False
why: This is session fixation. Issuing a new identifier at login invalidates the value the attacker holds.

q: In a federated login, once the identity provider disables a user, any account that was provisioned just in time in the service provider is always deleted automatically.
opts: True
False
why: Disabling the identity provider account stops new sign-ins, but local accounts, sessions or tokens in the service provider can persist unless deprovisioning (for example SCIM) is configured.

q: Service accounts should be included in access recertification and should have named owners.
opts: True
False
why: Service accounts are often over-privileged and forgotten. An owner, a documented purpose and periodic review are standard controls.

q: Which TWO controls reduce the risk of session hijacking? (Choose two.)
opts: Sending session cookies only over TLS with the Secure and HttpOnly attributes
Issuing a very long session lifetime so users rarely sign in again
Short idle and absolute session timeouts
Placing the session identifier in the page URL for easier debugging
Using the same session identifier before and after login
why: Protecting the cookie in transit and from scripts, and limiting its lifetime, both reduce the chance and impact of theft. Long lifetimes, URL identifiers and reuse across login all increase the exposure.

q: Which TWO are good practices for managing service accounts? (Choose two.)
opts: Grant only the permissions the application needs
Share the password among everyone who maintains the application
Exclude them from access reviews because they are not people
Use managed or vaulted credentials that are rotated automatically
Allow interactive logon so engineers can troubleshoot as the account
why: Automatic rotation and least privilege reduce theft and misuse. Interactive logon, shared passwords and exclusion from reviews erode accountability and let privileges drift.

q: A retailer is evaluating a payment processor and wants strong assurance that the processor's security controls actually operated effectively over the past year. Which report should the retailer request?
opts: A SOC 2 Type I report
A SOC 3 report
A SOC 2 Type II report
A SOC 1 Type I report
why: A SOC 2 Type II report tests the operating effectiveness of security-related controls over a period, which is the assurance requested. Type I only describes control design at a single date. SOC 3 is a general-use summary with little detail, and SOC 1 addresses controls over financial reporting rather than security.

q: A manager asks for the cheapest way to learn which servers are missing patches across the data center. Which activity BEST meets this need?
opts: A credentialed vulnerability scan
A red-team exercise
A full-scope penetration test
A social engineering test
why: A credentialed vulnerability scan logs in to hosts and reports missing patches and weak settings accurately and cheaply. A red-team exercise and a penetration test are slower and costlier and aim to demonstrate exploitation paths, not enumerate every missing patch. Social engineering tests people, not patch levels.

q: Before a penetration test of production systems begins, which item must be obtained FIRST?
opts: A list of all vulnerabilities found in the most recent scan of the environment
Written authorization with scope and rules of engagement
Administrator credentials for every system that is in scope for testing
A signed statement from management that no outages are possible
why: Written authorization and rules of engagement make the testing legal and define scope, timing and escalation. Past scan results and credentials may be useful later, and no tester can guarantee zero impact, so demanding that guarantee is unrealistic.

q: A tester is given a normal user account and basic network diagrams, then asked to see how far an insider could go. What type of test is this?
opts: White box
Gray box
Black box
Blind
why: Partial knowledge, such as a user-level account and limited documentation, is gray box testing. White box gives full knowledge including source and architecture, and black box gives none. Blind tests are one where the tester has no information and, in a double-blind variant, the defenders are not told either.

q: A scanner reports a critical vulnerability on an internal server. A senior engineer believes it is a false positive. What should the security analyst do NEXT?
opts: Ignore the finding because the senior engineer outranks the scanner's output
Immediately take the server offline to be safe until the vendor responds
Validate the finding by manual verification or another method
Lower the scanner's sensitivity globally to reduce future noise and workload
why: Findings should be validated before remediation effort is spent, using manual checks, credentialed verification or another tool. Ignoring it relies on opinion, and taking production offline without validation is disruptive. Lowering sensitivity globally increases the chance of false negatives.

q: Which metric is the BEST example of a key risk indicator for the vulnerability management program?
opts: Number of vulnerability scans run each month across all networks
Number of security training slides updated each quarter by the team
Average time analysts spend in meetings about vulnerability reports
Critical vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems past their deadline
why: A KRI signals rising exposure, and overdue critical vulnerabilities on exposed systems say how much risk is accumulating. Scan counts and meeting time measure activity, not risk, and training slide updates are unrelated to exposure.

q: A development team wants to find input-handling flaws and crashes in a file parser for which they have no source code. Which technique is MOST appropriate?
opts: Fuzzing the parser with malformed files
Static analysis of the source code
Peer review of the design documents
Interviewing the original developers
why: Fuzzing sends unexpected or malformed input to a running program and needs no source, which makes it well suited to a closed parser. Static analysis and design review need access to code or documents that are unavailable, and interviews would not find actual defects.

q: The auditors who will report to the board on the effectiveness of the security program must give an unbiased opinion. Which arrangement BEST supports that?
opts: Auditors who report to the chief information security officer being audited
Auditors independent of the audited functions, reporting to the board
Auditors who are also responsible for operating the controls under audit
Auditors selected and directed by the managers of the audited departments
why: Independence and a reporting line outside the audited function protect objectivity. Reporting to the person being audited, operating the controls they audit, or being chosen by those audited all create conflicts of interest.

q: After a penetration test, the report is a 300-page list of raw scanner output. The CEO asks what it means. What should the security manager have ensured the report contained?
opts: A longer list of every informational finding for the sake of completeness
Only the names of the testers, the dates tested and the tools used
An executive summary with prioritized, business-impact-based findings
A promise that all vulnerabilities have now been fixed and verified
why: Good reports translate technical results into business risk for the audience and give prioritized recommendations with owners. A longer unfiltered list buries the important issues, names and dates are not findings, and a test cannot promise that everything is fixed.

q: A company wants to verify that its detection tooling would catch common attacker techniques, repeatedly and without scheduling a consultant each time. Which approach BEST fits?
opts: An annual internal audit of the policy library
A reciprocal agreement with another company
A single penetration test at year end
Breach and attack simulation tooling run on a schedule
why: Breach and attack simulation safely replays attack techniques on a schedule to confirm preventive and detective controls work. A yearly pen test is infrequent, a policy audit does not exercise technical controls, and a reciprocal agreement is a continuity arrangement.

q: A project manager asks whether continuous monitoring can replace the three-year system reauthorization. What is the BEST answer?
opts: Yes, it provides ongoing evidence that supports ongoing authorization
No, because monitoring works only for network devices and not for applications
No, because reauthorization is legally required every three years in all cases
Yes, because once a system is authorized it never needs reviewing again
why: Information security continuous monitoring supplies near-real-time evidence of control status and risk, supporting ongoing authorization instead of point-in-time snapshots. It is not limited to network devices. Monitoring does not mean no further review, and the assertion of a universal three-year legal requirement is incorrect.

q: A new release has just fixed a security bug in the login module. Which testing activity BEST ensures that later changes do not reintroduce the bug?
opts: Regression tests including a case for the fixed flaw
A one-time penetration test of the whole network after release
Increasing the password length requirement for all users
A tabletop exercise for the incident response team next quarter
why: Regression tests re-run earlier checks, so adding a test for the specific flaw prevents it from silently returning. A network pen test, password change and tabletop exercise do not protect the code against regression.

q: The security team presents patching statistics to executives. Which presentation is MOST effective?
opts: A table listing every host with its patch level and last scan date
A trend of critical systems patched within policy deadlines, with the risk of late ones
The raw output of the patch management console for the whole estate
A walkthrough of how the patch tool works internally and its architecture
why: Executives need a measure tied to policy and risk, shown over time and with a clear implication. Raw host tables and console output are too detailed to support decisions, and tool internals do not address risk.

q: An organization wants to confirm that its web application resists abuse by testing scenarios such as bypassing the checkout approval step. Which technique describes this?
opts: Misuse case testing
Load testing
Usability testing
Synthetic availability monitoring
why: Misuse case testing explores how a feature could be abused and checks that controls hold. Load testing measures performance, usability testing looks at user experience, and synthetic monitoring checks availability and response, none of which target abuse of logic.

q: Which two statements correctly distinguish a vulnerability assessment from a penetration test? (Choose two.)
opts: A vulnerability assessment identifies and ranks weaknesses without necessarily exploiting them
A penetration test attempts to exploit weaknesses to show real impact
A vulnerability assessment always requires the testers to have no authorization
A penetration test produces no written report
A vulnerability assessment proves the business impact of chained attacks
why: Assessments find and prioritize, while penetration tests prove impact by exploiting. Both need authorization, and a report is the key deliverable of a pen test. Demonstrating chained impact is a penetration-testing strength, not an assessment feature.

q: Which two items belong in the rules of engagement for a penetration test? (Choose two.)
opts: Systems and network ranges that are in scope and out of scope
Testing windows and emergency contacts for stopping the test
The personal passwords of the system administrators
A waiver releasing the testers from any reporting duties
A list of production data the testers may copy for their own use
why: Rules of engagement set scope, timing, techniques and escalation contacts. Administrators' personal passwords should never be shared, testers must report their findings, and copying production data for personal use would be improper.

q: A SaaS provider offers a SOC 2 Type II report. Which two considerations should a customer reviewing it check? (Choose two.)
opts: Whether the audit period and trust criteria cover the services the customer actually uses
Whether exceptions and qualified opinions are noted and understood, including complementary user entity controls
Whether the report is a public marketing summary suitable for broad release
Whether it covers the customer's own internal network controls
Whether it proves that no breach can ever occur
why: A SOC 2 report is only as useful as its scope and findings, and the customer must also implement the user entity controls the report assumes. SOC 2 reports are restricted-use, not marketing summaries, and they cover the provider's service rather than the customer's network. No audit proves a breach is impossible.

q: A SOC 2 Type I report provides stronger assurance than a Type II report because it examines the controls in more detail.
opts: True
False
why: A Type I report covers design at a single point in time. A Type II also tests operating effectiveness over a period, which is stronger assurance.

q: A vulnerability scanner that reports a vulnerability that does not exist has produced a false positive.
opts: True
False
why: A false positive is a reported problem that is not real. Validation prevents wasted remediation effort.

q: A CVSS base score tells you exactly how much risk a vulnerability poses to your specific organization.
opts: True
False
why: CVSS expresses the technical severity of a flaw in general. Actual risk depends on your asset value, exposure, existing controls and whether exploitation is occurring.

q: In a gray box test, the tester is given partial knowledge of the target, such as a low-privilege account.
opts: True
False
why: Gray box sits between black box (no knowledge) and white box (full knowledge), and a user-level account is the usual example.

q: A clean static analysis report proves that an application has no security vulnerabilities.
opts: True
False
why: Static analysis reads code without running it, so it misses runtime, configuration and many logic problems, and it can produce false negatives. It complements dynamic testing, reviews and penetration tests rather than proving security.

q: An internal audit performed by the organization's own staff generally carries more credibility with outside regulators than an audit by an independent external firm.
opts: True
False
why: External independent audits carry more weight with regulators and customers. Internal audits are valuable for readiness and improvement but are less independent.

q: A new security manager must plan assessments for the coming year. Which approach BEST forms the basis of the strategy?
opts: Test the easiest systems first so that the coverage percentage looks high in the annual report
Repeat last year's tests exactly, to give comparable results from one year to the next
Test only the systems that have failed audits in the past and ignore everything else
Prioritize testing by risk and requirements, and validate that results drive remediation
why: A strategy derived from risk and compliance needs, with a feedback check that findings are acted on, directs effort where it matters. Testing the easy systems, repeating tests unchanged or looking only at past failures leaves new and untested risks unaddressed.

q: A company wants to run a penetration test against its workloads in a public cloud. Which step comes FIRST?
opts: Ask the provider to disable its logging during the test
Test the provider's hypervisors because they are part of the same account
Review the provider's permitted-testing policy and obtain internal written authorization
Begin scanning the provider's shared network ranges to find weaknesses
why: The customer may test only what it controls and must follow the provider's rules, in addition to its own authorization. Scanning shared ranges, disabling provider logging and attacking hypervisors are outside the customer's remit and may violate the terms of service.

q: A security team collects logs from every system but nobody examines them unless an incident happens. Which change MOST improves the value of the logs as a control?
opts: Allow administrators to edit logs so they can fix errors
Define what is reviewed, who reviews it and how often, automating correlation and alerts
Collect logs from even more systems and applications without changing review procedures, since a larger data set will eventually reveal every problem
Reduce the retention period so there are fewer logs to examine
why: Logs become a control only when reviewed against defined expectations. Collecting more without review adds volume, shortening retention loses evidence and editable logs undermine integrity.

q: An e-commerce company wants to know quickly when the checkout process stops working at night, before customers complain. Which technique is BEST?
opts: Scripted synthetic transactions that run on a schedule from outside locations
A static analysis scan of the checkout source code each quarter
A one-time penetration test of the checkout page
An annual SOC 2 audit of the hosting provider
why: Synthetic transactions exercise the real flow continuously and alert on failures. Static analysis, annual penetration tests and annual audits are periodic and cannot show current availability.

q: A test team reports 98 percent code coverage and says the application is therefore secure. How should the security manager respond?
opts: Accept the claim because 98 percent leaves too little room for flaws
Ask for 100 percent coverage, which then guarantees the application is secure and removes the need for any other security testing activities
Ignore coverage, because it has no relationship to testing quality
Coverage shows how much code was exercised, not that the tests checked for security flaws or covered misuse
why: High coverage means most code ran during tests, not that the tests included hostile input, abuse cases or logic checks. Accepting the claim confuses activity with assurance, even 100 percent does not prove security, and coverage is still a useful gap indicator.

q: A scan shows port 22 open, port 23 filtered and port 80 closed on a server. Which statement is correct?
opts: All three ports are open but only port 22 accepted a connection
The scan proves that SSH is vulnerable on port 22
A service is listening on port 22, while a device such as a firewall appears to block probes to port 23
Ports 22 and 23 are both listening for connections, while port 80 is blocked by a firewall that drops the probes sent by the scanner
why: Open means a service answered, closed means the host responded that nothing listens and filtered means no clear response, typically because of a firewall. An open port is not proof of vulnerability, and the other statements misread the states.

q: A vulnerability team has 2,000 findings. Which approach to prioritization is BEST?
opts: Fix findings in the order they were discovered, regardless of severity, exploitation evidence, exposure or the importance of the affected systems
Combine severity with exploitation evidence, asset value and exposure, for example using EPSS and the CISA known-exploited list
Fix findings in alphabetical order of the host name
Fix only findings with a base score of 10 and ignore all others
why: Prioritization works when severity is combined with real-world exploitation likelihood and business context. Alphabetical or first-in order ignores risk, and a cutoff of 10 ignores actively exploited findings with lower scores.

q: A manager wants a structured reference for planning and reporting a penetration test, not merely a list of tools. Which is MOST appropriate?
opts: An accounting standard for financial statements
A methodology such as PTES, OSSTMM or NIST SP 800-115
The vendor's marketing brochure for its scanner
The company's employee handbook
why: Recognized penetration testing methodologies structure scoping, execution, evidence and reporting. Marketing material, a handbook and a financial reporting standard do not describe security testing practice.

q: A review of security process data finds 120 active accounts that match no current employee, while the leaver process appears complete on paper. Which conclusion is MOST accurate?
opts: The leaver control is not operating effectively, and the evidence should be reported with a remediation plan
The process works because documents say so
The accounts are harmless as long as no one has reported abuse
The count is acceptable because 120 is a small fraction of all accounts, and the leaver process is documented, approved and reviewed each year
why: Process data shows what actually happens, and orphaned accounts demonstrate that the control failed in practice. Documentation alone does not prove operation, unused accounts remain attack paths and size does not excuse a control failure.

q: An application owner cannot patch a legacy system for six months because of a vendor dependency. Which handling is BEST?
opts: Close the finding without further action since patching is not possible
Hide the system from the scanner so the finding disappears from the weekly report
Accept the risk permanently in an email from the system administrator to the help desk
Record a time-limited exception with compensating controls, owner approval and a review date
why: A managed exception keeps the risk visible, reduces it with compensating controls and forces a revisit. Closing the finding or hiding the system conceals risk, and a permanent informal acceptance by an administrator lacks authority and expiry.

q: A researcher discovers a flaw in a vendor's product and wants to follow responsible practice. Which sequence BEST matches coordinated disclosure?
opts: Sell the flaw to the highest bidder before the vendor knows
Tell only the vendor's competitors so that they can review the product and compete on security, without informing the vendor or its customers first
Report privately to the vendor, allow time to fix, then publish details after the agreed period
Publish the exploit immediately so that all users are aware at once
why: Coordinated disclosure protects users by giving the vendor time to develop a fix before details are public. Immediate publication, selling the flaw and informing competitors all harm users or are unethical.

q: During an external audit, the auditee proposes to select the sample of invoices that the auditor will test. What is the BEST response?
opts: Test only the invoices that were already corrected before the audit, because the auditee has confirmed that these are accurate and complete
The auditor should select the sample independently using a risk-based or statistical method
Accept the sample, because the auditee knows the invoices best
Refuse to test anything and ask for a signed statement instead
why: Auditor-selected samples preserve independence and ensure representativeness. Auditee-chosen samples can hide problems, a statement is weak evidence and testing only corrected items would bias results.

q: A new customer asks a SaaS vendor for evidence of its controls. The vendor holds an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate and a SOC 2 Type II report. Which statement is MOST accurate?
opts: The certificate shows a conforming management system, while the SOC 2 Type II report describes tested controls over a period
Both documents prove that the vendor cannot be breached, so no further due diligence or contractual protection is needed for the new customer
The SOC 2 report is a certificate issued by ISO
The ISO certificate lists every control test result in detail
why: These are different assurance forms: certification of an information security management system versus an attestation report with tested controls. Neither proves immunity, SOC 2 comes from an AICPA-based auditor and the certificate itself does not list test results.

q: A low-severity CVSS base score means a vulnerability can safely be ignored on an internet-facing system that attackers are actively exploiting.
opts: True
False
why: Active exploitation and exposure can make a low-scored flaw the highest priority. Base scores describe intrinsic severity, not your risk.

q: A security.txt file published on a website tells researchers where and how to report vulnerabilities.
opts: True
False
why: security.txt (RFC 9116) is served from the /.well-known/ path and lists contact details and the disclosure policy, which makes coordinated disclosure easier. It is a convenience and not a legal safe harbor.

q: An exception to a security requirement should have a documented justification, compensating controls and an expiry or review date.
opts: True
False
why: Exceptions are managed risk acceptance. Without expiry and compensating controls they become permanent, unmanaged gaps.

q: An ISO/IEC 27001 certificate is issued after a single audit and remains valid indefinitely without further audits.
opts: True
False
why: Certification uses a stage 1 and stage 2 audit, followed by annual surveillance audits and recertification after three years.

q: Which TWO are appropriate inputs to a management review of the security program? (Choose two.)
opts: The color scheme of the security dashboard
Audit results and the status of previous corrective actions
Only the number of firewall rules, without context
Incident trends and changes in the risk landscape
Personal opinions of the security team about each employee
why: Management review needs audit and action status plus incidents and risk changes so decisions can be made. Raw counts without context, opinions about employees and visual styling do not inform governance decisions.

q: Which TWO practices make a penetration test safer for production systems? (Choose two.)
opts: Use real customer data in the test environment without masking
Skip written authorization because verbal approval is enough
Agree test windows and an emergency contact before starting
Run exploits freely during peak business hours without notice
Have backups and a rollback plan ready
why: Agreed windows, contacts, backups and rollback limit harm if something fails. Unannounced peak-hour exploitation, unmasked real data and missing written authorization increase risk or create legal exposure.

q: A responder arrives at a running server suspected of compromise and must preserve evidence for possible prosecution. Which collection order is CORRECT?
opts: Disk image first, then memory, then network connections and logs
Memory and running state, then disk, then archived backups
Archived backups first, then disk, then memory and running processes
Shut the server down immediately, then image the disk for analysis
why: Evidence is collected from most to least volatile: memory, processes and network state first, then disk, then remote logs and archives. Imaging disk first loses memory contents, and shutting down destroys volatile data that may show the attacker's activity.

q: After a suspected data theft, investigators want to know exactly which files an attacker copied out of the network, but the organization keeps only flow records (source, destination, ports and byte counts). What is the main limitation of this evidence?
opts: Flow records show who talked to whom, when and how much, but not the content that was transferred
Flow records cannot be matched with time stamps from other systems even when the clocks are synchronized
Flow records are inadmissible in any court because the network devices generate them automatically
Flow records are rewritten by the network devices whenever the traffic they describe is encrypted
why: Flow data is metadata: it shows who communicated with whom, when and in what volume, which helps spot unusual destinations, but it cannot show file contents. Content needs full packet capture or host and application logs, and encrypted payloads may stay unreadable. Flow records can be correlated using synchronized time, are accepted as evidence when collected and protected properly, and are not changed by encryption.

q: During an investigation, evidence was left in an unlocked cabinet for two days and no record exists of who had access. What is the MOST likely consequence?
opts: The evidence becomes more reliable because it was never moved
The hash values will automatically change
The evidence will be treated as classified information
A broken chain of custody may make the evidence inadmissible
why: Chain of custody documents who handled the evidence and when. Gaps allow a challenger to argue it could have been altered, risking exclusion. Leaving it unmonitored does not make it more reliable, hashes change only if the data changes, and classification is a different matter.

q: A SIEM generates thousands of low-value alerts daily, and analysts are missing real incidents. What is the BEST improvement?
opts: Disable all alerting and review the logs manually once a month
Tune correlation rules and prioritize alerts by asset criticality
Double the number of log sources without changing any of the rules
Reduce log retention so that there is less data to search
why: Alert fatigue is solved by tuning and prioritization with context, so analysts see what matters. Disabling alerts removes detection, more sources without tuning adds noise, and shortening retention harms investigations without reducing alerts.

q: Investigators cannot correlate events across a firewall, server and application because timestamps differ by several minutes. Which control would have prevented this?
opts: Longer log retention periods on the central collector
Encryption of the log files at rest on each server
More verbose logging levels on the application servers
Synchronizing all systems to a trusted time source
why: Correlation depends on consistent timestamps, which comes from synchronization with a trusted source such as NTP. Retention, encryption and verbosity are useful but do not fix clock differences.

q: A company discovers that an administrator edited the logs of a server he manages to hide a configuration change. Which control would BEST have prevented this?
opts: Forwarding logs in real time to a store the administrator cannot modify
Increasing the administrator's password length and adding complexity rules
Requiring the administrator to complete annual security awareness training
Rotating the administrator to a different team at the end of each year
why: Forwarding logs immediately to a protected central repository, with separation from the people being logged, preserves integrity and accountability. A longer password, training and job rotation might deter or detect later but do not stop log alteration.

q: A security analyst notices that a workstation is communicating with a known malicious address. According to the incident response lifecycle, what is the FIRST action once the event is confirmed as an incident?
opts: Rebuild the workstation from a clean image immediately to remove the threat
Publish a press statement to reassure customers and regulators
Update the incident response plan to reflect the new threat
Contain the affected system while preserving evidence
why: After detection and analysis confirm an incident, containment limits damage while evidence is preserved. Rebuilding first destroys evidence and may leave the root cause unknown, press statements go through the communications process, and plan updates come in lessons learned.

q: Which phase of incident response is MOST important to complete BEFORE any incident occurs?
opts: Eradication
Lessons learned
Preparation
Recovery
why: Preparation, meaning the plan, trained team, tools, contacts and logging, determines the quality of everything else and has to be done in advance. The other phases occur during or after an incident.

q: After removing ransomware from several servers, the team wants to bring services back. What should they do to reduce the chance of reinfection?
opts: Restore from a known-good backup, after closing the entry vector, and monitor
Restore the most recent backup without checking when the infection began
Reconnect the servers to the network first and scan them afterward while users work
Pay the ransom to make the attacker stop and provide the decryption key
why: Recovery should use clean data, with the root cause fixed and heightened monitoring. The latest backup may already be infected, reconnecting before verification invites reinfection, and paying does not guarantee removal or return of data.

q: A change to a production firewall rule caused an outage. The engineer says it was urgent and so no approval was needed. What is the BEST response from the change management perspective?
opts: Reward the engineer for acting quickly under pressure and skipping approvals
Remove the firewall from change control to avoid future delays
Define an expedited emergency path with retrospective review
Prohibit all emergency changes regardless of business impact
why: Real emergencies need a defined fast path that still records, approves and reviews the change afterward. Rewarding bypass undermines control, removing the firewall from control increases risk, and banning emergency changes is unworkable.

q: A critical patch for an actively exploited vulnerability has been released. The change advisory board next meets in three weeks. What is the BEST course of action?
opts: Wait for the next scheduled meeting in three weeks regardless of the risk
Apply the patch to all systems immediately without any testing at all
Ignore the patch because the systems are protected behind a firewall
Use the emergency change process with quick testing and a rollback plan
why: An actively exploited flaw justifies an expedited change with minimal but real testing and rollback readiness. Waiting weeks leaves exposure, skipping testing risks outages, and a firewall alone does not remove the vulnerability.

q: A hospital's billing system has an RTO of four hours and an RPO of 30 minutes. Which backup and recovery approach BEST fits?
opts: Weekly full backups to tape that are stored at an offsite location
Frequent replication or log shipping to a warm or hot site
Monthly backups combined with a cold site that must be built first
A reciprocal agreement with another hospital with no testing
why: A 30-minute RPO needs near-continuous replication or very frequent backups, and a four-hour RTO needs a site that is largely ready. Weekly tape and a cold site would lose too much data and take too long, and an untested reciprocal arrangement is unreliable.

q: The restore process must be as quick as possible while keeping daily backup windows short. Which scheme is BEST suited?
opts: Full backup on Sunday with daily differential backups
Full backup on Sunday with daily incremental backups
Daily full backups only
Incremental backups with no full backup
why: With differentials, a restore needs only the last full and the most recent differential, and the daily backup is smaller than a full. Incrementals give the shortest backup window but a longer restore, daily fulls have long windows, and incrementals with no full cannot restore at all.

q: After successful parallel tests, management wants proof that the alternate site can carry the live workload and accepts the risk of a short outage in exchange. Which test type gives the MOST realistic evidence?
opts: Full interruption test
Parallel test
Read-through test
Tabletop discussion
why: A full interruption test actually shuts down production and runs operations from the alternate site, which makes it the most realistic proof and also the riskiest, so it needs management approval and a rollback plan. A parallel test runs recovery alongside production without proving the site can carry the load alone, and a read-through and a tabletop discussion do not exercise real recovery.

q: A technician finds a small fire in an energized server rack in the data center. Which type of portable extinguisher is appropriate?
opts: A water extinguisher, because water absorbs the most heat from the equipment
A carbon dioxide or clean-agent extinguisher rated for electrical fires
A wet chemical extinguisher, because it is designed for cooking oils and fats
A foam extinguisher, because foam smothers every type of fire
why: Energized electrical equipment is a Class C fire, and carbon dioxide and clean-agent extinguishers do not conduct electricity and leave little or no residue. Water and foam conduct current and risk shock and equipment damage, and wet chemical agents are designed for Class K cooking fires.

q: In a small finance team one clerk has handled the same payment process for years and nobody else understands it. This lets hidden fraud continue and leaves no backup when the clerk is absent. Which control BEST addresses both problems?
opts: A longer password policy for finance staff
A larger firewall at the network perimeter
Additional antivirus software on finance workstations
Job rotation with cross-training between team members
why: Rotating people through roles lets a second person see the process, so irregularities surface, and cross-training provides coverage during absences. Passwords, firewalls and antivirus do not address insider fraud that stays hidden because one person always controls a process.

q: Which two actions are appropriate during containment of a suspected malware incident on a server? (Choose two.)
opts: Isolate the server from the network while preserving its memory and disk state for analysis
Document actions and timestamps in an incident log
Immediately wipe the server to remove the malware
Notify the attacker that they have been detected
Delete log files to reduce storage usage
why: Containment stops spread while preserving evidence, and documentation supports later analysis and legal needs. Wiping immediately destroys evidence and root cause information, alerting the attacker may cause more damage, and deleting logs destroys the record.

q: Which two statements about backup types are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: A differential backup copies data changed since the last full backup
An incremental backup copies data changed since the last backup of any type
A differential backup needs every previous differential to restore
A full backup copies only changed files
Incremental backups give the fastest restore
why: Differentials are relative to the last full and incrementals to the last backup of any type. A differential restore needs only the last full and the latest differential, a full backup copies everything, and incrementals are quickest to take but slowest to restore.

q: Which two items should be reviewed in a post-incident lessons-learned session? (Choose two.)
opts: What allowed the incident to occur and which controls failed or worked
Which detection and response steps were slow and what to change
Which employee to blame so they can be dismissed
How to conceal the incident from regulators
Whether to delete the incident log
why: Lessons learned finds root cause and process improvements. Reviews are blameless, concealment from regulators may be illegal, and deleting the incident record removes evidence and organizational learning.

q: Which two controls help ensure that backups will survive a ransomware attack? (Choose two.)
opts: Immutable or offline copies that cannot be modified or deleted from the production network
Separate credentials for backup systems that production administrators cannot use
Storing backups on a share that every server can write to
Using the domain administrator account for backup jobs
Skipping restore tests to avoid overwriting data
why: Ransomware seeks out and destroys reachable backups, so immutable or offline copies and separated credentials protect them. A widely writable share, a domain administrator account and untested backups all increase risk.

q: An event is any observable occurrence in a system, and every event should be treated as an incident.
opts: True
False
why: An event is any observable occurrence, and only those that actually or potentially violate policy or threaten confidentiality, integrity or availability are incidents. Triage separates the two.

q: When collecting evidence from a live system, volatile data such as memory should be collected before disk contents.
opts: True
False
why: Memory and running state disappear on shutdown or change quickly, so the order of volatility puts them first.

q: The maximum tolerable downtime must be shorter than the recovery time objective.
opts: True
False
why: The RTO must fit within the MTD, so the MTD is the larger limit. The RTO plus work recovery time must not exceed the MTD.

q: RAID provides adequate protection against ransomware and accidental file deletion.
opts: True
False
why: RAID provides redundancy against disk failure but replicates deletions and encrypted data. Backups, especially offline or immutable ones, address those threats.

q: A tabletop exercise is a discussion-based test that does not disrupt production systems.
opts: True
False
why: Tabletops walk participants through a scenario verbally, so they are inexpensive and safe, though they do not prove technical recovery works.

q: Destroying records that are under a legal hold can be spoliation of evidence even if the destruction followed the normal retention schedule.
opts: True
False
why: Once litigation is reasonably anticipated, the duty to preserve overrides the retention schedule. Destroying relevant records afterwards, even through an automatic deletion job, can lead to court sanctions.

q: Application allow listing is generally stronger than block listing because it denies unknown software by default.
opts: True
False
why: Block lists must anticipate every bad program, while allow lists permit only approved software, so new malware is blocked without an update.

q: A security analyst suspects an employee of leaking trade secrets. HR wants to start by confronting the employee. What should the investigator do FIRST?
opts: Confront the employee so they can explain before any evidence is gathered
Wipe the employee's laptop to prevent further leaks
Announce the investigation to the department to deter other staff
Engage legal counsel and secure relevant evidence before the employee is alerted
why: Involving counsel and securing evidence quietly keeps the investigation lawful and prevents destruction of evidence. Confronting first tips off the subject, wiping destroys evidence and announcing the matter harms confidentiality and fairness.

q: A forensic examiner's report states conclusions but does not record which tool version imaged the drive or its hash value. What is the MOST likely consequence?
opts: The report is admissible without questions because examiners are trusted
The hash value is unnecessary once the drive is in a locked cabinet
The credibility and reproducibility of the findings may be challenged
The evidence automatically becomes stronger because it is simpler
why: Documentation of tools, versions and hashes lets another examiner reproduce results and show the image is authentic. Omitting them weakens credibility, trust in the examiner is not a substitute, and a locked cabinet does not prove integrity.

q: A responder seizes a smartphone that may contain evidence and is connected to the corporate mobile management system. What should be done IMMEDIATELY?
opts: Ask the owner to unlock it and delete personal photos first
Isolate it from networks with a Faraday bag or equivalent and keep it powered while documenting its state
Power it off to preserve the battery and put it in a drawer until the case is assigned and an examiner is available to begin the work
Reset it to factory settings to remove corporate data
why: Network isolation prevents remote wipe or changes while preserving volatile state. Powering off can lose data or trigger encryption locks, a factory reset destroys evidence and asking the owner to delete content alters it.

q: A company suspects slow, steady data theft over encrypted web traffic from a workstation. Which capability would MOST help detect this?
opts: Egress monitoring with volume and destination baselines and DLP on outbound channels
Increasing the length and complexity of user passwords, together with a shorter expiry period for all accounts across the whole organization
Adding more physical guards at the building entrance
Disabling the host firewall to speed up transfers
why: Monitoring the outbound path against baselines reveals unusual volumes or destinations, and DLP checks content where inspection is permitted. Password length, guards and disabling the host firewall do nothing to detect exfiltration.

q: An investigation cannot establish when a firewall rule change happened because device logs show different times and some logs are missing. Which improvement addresses BOTH problems?
opts: Delete older logs to avoid inconsistencies
Forward logs to a central, access-controlled collector over reliable transport with synchronized time
Allow each administrator to keep their own copy of the logs locally on the device they manage, so that every team can search them quickly
Turn on verbose logging only after an incident is suspected
why: Central collection with reliable transport prevents loss, and NTP synchronization makes events comparable. Local copies keep inconsistent and editable records, enabling logging only after suspicion misses the cause, and deleting logs destroys evidence.

q: A SOC adopts a machine-learning tool that automatically isolates hosts it considers suspicious. After a model update it isolates a payroll server during pay run. What is the BEST lesson?
opts: Keep human approval for impactful actions, validate models after changes and monitor for drift
Never use machine learning in the SOC again because automation always causes outages
Allow the tool to act without review since it is more accurate than people
Disable logging of the tool's decisions to reduce noise and storage costs for the SOC
why: AI tools need validation, drift monitoring and human oversight for high-impact actions. Rejecting them entirely forgoes value, unreviewed automation causes outages and removing logs removes the ability to learn and audit.

q: A company builds servers manually and finds that no two have the same settings. Which approach BEST provides consistent, auditable configuration?
opts: Let each administrator document their own build steps in a personal notebook, which keeps the knowledge close to the person who does the work
Apply the same configuration only to the servers that failed an audit
Remove the baseline so that administrators have more flexibility
Provision from hardened templates or infrastructure as code and detect drift against the baseline
why: Templates, code-driven builds and drift detection give repeatable, reviewable configuration. Personal notebooks, partial application and removing baselines all prevent consistency.

q: A company outsources its help desk and wants to ensure the provider restores service quickly and handles security incidents properly. Which instrument BEST sets measurable expectations?
opts: The provider's marketing statement about quality
A policy for internal staff only
A service-level agreement with response, restoration and security reporting targets
A verbal promise from the account manager, confirmed in a friendly email, that the provider will do its best to restore service quickly
why: An SLA defines measurable commitments and consequences. Verbal promises, marketing claims and internal policies are not enforceable or measurable for the provider.

q: A systems administrator performs email, web browsing and administrative tasks all from one account that has domain administrator rights. What is the BEST change?
opts: Increase the lockout threshold on the account
Use a separate privileged account only for administration, from a hardened workstation, with logging
Remove the administrator's ability to browse the web in the future, and allow email only from the same account to avoid a second login
Share the administrator account with a colleague for backup
why: Separating accounts and hardening the admin path limits credential theft from everyday risks. Removing browsing is not practical, sharing worsens accountability and a higher lockout threshold does not address exposure.

q: A company stores backup tapes in a courier's van between buildings. Which control BEST protects the data if a tape is lost?
opts: Encrypt the backup media and track it with tamper-evident packaging and a handoff log
Label the tape with the word "confidential" in large letters and ask the courier to sign a form promising to handle it with great care
Rely on the courier's reputation for safe delivery
Delete the backup index so nobody can read it
why: Encryption protects the content, and tracking and tamper-evident packaging add accountability. A label does not protect data, reputation is not a control and deleting the index does not stop access to the tape.

q: A company's incident response plan says nothing about who may speak to regulators or the press. During an incident, three executives give different statements. What is the BEST improvement?
opts: Ask all staff to share updates on social media
Avoid communicating with anyone outside the incident team until the incident is fully resolved and the root cause has been written up in detail
Allow the technical team to publish raw incident data
Define a communications plan with a single authorized spokesperson and legal review of notifications
why: A single spokesperson with legal review keeps messages consistent and compliant with notification duties. Social media updates, silence and raw data release each create legal, reputational or operational risk.

q: A kiosk system in a factory runs only three approved applications and never needs new software. Which control gives the BEST protection against unknown malware?
opts: Weekly manual reviews of the process list
A larger signature database updated monthly
Application allow listing so only approved programs can run
A deny list that blocks known malicious file names
why: For a fixed-function system, allow listing blocks anything not approved, including unknown malware. Deny lists and signatures only catch known items, and manual reviews are slow and error-prone.

q: A small company contracts a managed detection and response provider. After a breach, management says the provider is responsible for everything. Which statement is MOST accurate?
opts: The company has no ability to review the provider's performance
The company remains accountable and should have defined scope, response authority and audit rights in the contract
Accountability transfers entirely to the provider once the contract is signed, because the provider now runs monitoring and response on the customer's behalf
The provider must disclose breaches only to its own staff
why: Outsourcing operations does not outsource accountability, so contracts and oversight matter. Full transfer is a misconception, disclosure duties still exist and customers can audit and review service levels.

q: A critical server cannot be patched this month because the vendor has not certified the update. A scanner flags a remotely exploitable flaw. What is the BEST interim action?
opts: Apply compensating controls such as an IPS or WAF rule and isolation, record an exception and set a patch date
Ignore the finding until the vendor certifies the update, then schedule the patch for the next regular maintenance window several months from now
Disable the scanner so that the finding disappears
Patch immediately without testing to remove the finding
why: Compensating controls reduce exposure while a documented exception keeps the risk managed. Ignoring or hiding the finding leaves it exploitable, and untested patching risks outage.

q: A change to a production database was approved and implemented in the maintenance window, but it caused errors and the system must be returned to its earlier state quickly. Which part of the change request should have been prepared in advance?
opts: A documented and tested rollback (back-out) plan
An updated business impact analysis for the database
Additional logging on the database server
A larger change advisory board
why: A change request should say how to back out if the change fails: a documented and ideally tested rollback plan returns the system to its last known-good state quickly. An updated impact analysis, extra logging and a larger board may help with other things but do not restore service.

q: A company must restore a billing system within one hour of a regional disaster and cannot lose more than five minutes of data. Which design BEST meets these objectives?
opts: Weekly tape backups stored in a vault at the same site, with the tapes tested twice a year and replaced when they reach the end of their life
A cold site that can be equipped within two weeks
A reciprocal agreement with a neighbor that has no spare capacity
An active-active or hot standby site in another region with synchronous or near-synchronous replication
why: The recovery time and point objectives demand a geographically separate site that is current and ready. Weekly tapes, a cold site and an informal reciprocal arrangement cannot meet one hour or five minutes.

q: An organization has a service that must achieve 99.99 percent availability. Approximately how much downtime per year does this allow?
opts: About 5 minutes
About 3.7 days
About 53 minutes
About 8.8 hours
why: Availability of 99.99 percent leaves 0.01 percent of a year, about 53 minutes. About 8.8 hours corresponds to 99.9 percent, about 5 minutes to 99.999 percent and 3.7 days to 99 percent.

q: After a regional outage the DR team has restored services at the alternate site. Which order is the usual best practice when returning to the repaired primary site?
opts: Never return, because the alternate site is always better
Move the least critical systems back first, to test the primary site before critical ones follow
Move the most critical systems back first, to end the disruption for the business as quickly as possible and demonstrate that recovery is complete
Move everything at once, to save time
why: Moving less critical systems first proves the primary site works before risking critical services. Moving critical systems or everything at once increases risk, and permanent relocation is a business decision, not a rule.

q: A company's DR plan relies on email to notify staff of a disaster, but the email system is hosted in the affected data center. What is the BEST improvement?
opts: Add out-of-band communications such as mass notification and call trees with current contact lists
Send an email asking staff to test the plan
Remove the notification section from the plan
Store the contact list only on the affected servers, because they are the systems that the recovery team will repair and restore first
why: Communications must not depend on the failed systems, so alternate channels are required. An email test would fail, removing notification leaves a gap and storing contacts on affected servers repeats the problem.

q: A disaster recovery test at the alternate site has just finished. Most systems met their recovery objectives but two did not. Which activity MUST follow?
opts: Archive the plan unchanged, because most of the systems passed
Wait for next year's test before changing anything in the plan
Delete the test data and logs so that the results cannot be misused
Document the results and lessons learned, and update the plan to close the gaps
why: A test is only useful if its results are documented, the failures analyzed and the plan corrected, so the next test or a real event goes better. Leaving the plan unchanged repeats the failures, waiting a year leaves the gaps open, and deleting records removes the evidence needed for improvement and for auditors.

q: A data center has a 6-foot fence, but there are no cameras, no lighting and no guard patrol. A penetration tester climbs over it unnoticed. Which principle does this BEST illustrate?
opts: Lighting is only required in indoor areas
A 6-foot fence is sufficient for any threat
A barrier only delays unless something detects the intrusion and someone responds
Fences are never effective in any circumstances and should be removed, with the budget moved to guard salaries and an additional alarm contract
why: Delay without detection and response gives intruders time. Fences still serve a purpose when combined with surveillance, lighting is a perimeter control and a single fence height does not suit every threat.

q: A manager is traveling to a country with a high risk of device theft and surveillance. Which action BEST reduces the risk to company data?
opts: Leave the laptop unattended in the hotel room, secured with a cable lock
Carry a clean loaner device with minimal data, full-disk encryption and VPN access
Bring the primary laptop with all files on it and rely on the hotel safe at night
Use free public Wi-Fi and public charging kiosks to save on roaming and battery costs
why: A clean, encrypted device limits what can be lost or compromised. A full-data laptop, public Wi-Fi and kiosks, and an unattended laptop all create exposure.

q: An employee under threat from an intruder is asked to unlock the server room. The company wants them to be able to signal for help without alerting the intruder. Which control fits?
opts: A duress code or silent alarm that appears to grant normal access
A louder alarm that sounds throughout the building
A policy telling employees never to give access to anyone
A sign on the door telling intruders to leave
why: A duress signal alerts security while the person appears to comply, protecting life. A loud alarm may provoke the intruder, a never-comply policy puts people at risk and a sign is ineffective.

q: When a suspect phone is seized as evidence, it should be switched on and connected to the network so that it can synchronize before it is examined.
opts: True
False
why: A connected phone can be remotely wiped or altered. It should be isolated from networks, for example in a Faraday bag, while its state is documented.

q: An application allow list that identifies programs only by file name is as strong as one that uses cryptographic hashes or signed publisher certificates.
opts: True
False
why: File names are easily changed or copied by malware, so a name-based rule is trivially bypassed. Strong allow lists identify software by hash, publisher certificate or a protected install path.

q: Outsourcing security monitoring to a managed provider transfers legal accountability for breaches entirely to that provider.
opts: True
False
why: The customer remains accountable. Contracts, oversight and audit rights are how it manages the provider.

q: During return to the primary site after a disaster, the usual practice is to move the most critical systems first.
opts: True
False
why: The least critical systems usually return first so that problems at the repaired primary site are found before critical services depend on it.

q: Sandbox environments can be evaded by malware that detects it is being analyzed, so sandboxing should be combined with other detection controls.
opts: True
False
why: Some malware waits or behaves benignly in analysis environments. Layered detection compensates.

q: Which TWO actions should be taken when a suspect laptop is found running during an investigation? (Choose two.)
opts: Capture volatile memory before powering the system down
Run a disk cleanup tool to reduce clutter before imaging
Document the state of the screen and running processes
Restart the laptop to see whether the issue goes away
Install antivirus software on the laptop immediately
why: Volatile data and the observed state should be preserved first. Cleanup, restart and installing software change or destroy evidence.

q: Which TWO are correct statements about a service-level agreement with a security provider? (Choose two.)
opts: It should include reporting and audit rights
It is unnecessary if the provider is well known
It prevents any security incident from occurring
It should state measurable targets, such as response and restoration times
It makes the provider solely accountable for the customer's legal duties
why: Measurable targets and oversight rights make an SLA useful. It does not transfer accountability, reputation does not replace it and it cannot guarantee that incidents will not occur.

q: Which TWO design choices help a multi-site architecture meet a very low recovery point objective? (Choose two.)
opts: Rely on a reciprocal agreement with no capacity commitment
Replicate data synchronously or near-synchronously between sites
Back up once per month to tape
Keep sites far enough apart not to share a regional disaster
Place both sites in the same building
why: Frequent replication limits data loss and geographic separation protects against regional events. Monthly tape backups, a single building and uncommitted capacity do not meet a low RPO.

q: A product team has a security review scheduled one week before release in each cycle and keeps finding design flaws that delay the launch. Which change BEST addresses the root cause?
opts: Add another security review after release to catch what was missed
Hire more penetration testers for the final week before launch
Shift security left with requirements and design-stage threat modeling
Remove the final review so that releases are no longer delayed
why: Flaws found late are costly to fix, so security requirements and threat modeling during design find them early. More reviews at the end or after release do not remove the cost of late discovery, and removing review just ships the flaws.

q: A web page displays user comments exactly as submitted, and an attacker posts a comment containing a script that runs in other visitors' browsers. Which is the PRIMARY defense?
opts: Longer passwords for the people who post comments
Contextual output encoding of comments
Using a stronger database encryption algorithm for stored comments
Increasing the session timeout for logged-in users
why: This is stored cross-site scripting, and encoding data for the context where it is rendered makes the browser treat it as text, not script. Password length, database encryption and session timeout do not stop script injection.

q: A developer builds a SQL query by joining strings with user input. Which control BEST prevents SQL injection?
opts: Removing quotation marks and semicolons from all user input
Hiding detailed database error messages from the web page only
Encrypting the network connection between application and database
Parameterized queries with a least-privileged database account
why: Parameterization separates code from data so input can never change the query structure, and least privilege limits damage if something slips through. Stripping characters is bypassable, hiding errors only reduces information leakage, and encrypting the connection protects traffic, not query logic.

q: An attacker tricks a logged-in banking customer into clicking a link that silently submits a transfer request using the customer's active session. Which defense is MOST specific to this attack?
opts: Anti-CSRF tokens validated on state-changing requests
Contextual output encoding of all user-supplied content on the page
Rate limiting on the login page to slow credential guessing
Disabling directory listing on the web server's document folders
why: This is cross-site request forgery, which is stopped by unpredictable per-session tokens (plus SameSite cookies) that an attacker cannot supply. Output encoding addresses XSS, login rate limiting addresses guessing, and directory listing is unrelated.

q: A program checks that a file is writable by the user and then, a moment later, opens it. An attacker swaps the file with a link to a protected file between the two steps. What flaw is this?
opts: Buffer overflow
Time-of-check to time-of-use race condition
Cross-site scripting
Insecure deserialization
why: The state changed between the check and its use, which is a TOCTOU race condition, fixed by making the check and use atomic. A buffer overflow writes beyond memory bounds, XSS runs script in a browser, and deserialization flaws involve untrusted serialized objects.

q: An organization wants to find vulnerabilities in a running web application, including configuration and authentication problems, without access to source code. Which tool type fits?
opts: Static application security testing
Software composition analysis
Dynamic application security testing
Peer code review
why: Dynamic testing attacks the running application from outside and finds runtime and configuration issues. Static testing and peer review need source, and composition analysis inventories third-party components rather than probing behavior.

q: A critical vulnerability is announced in a widely used open-source logging library. The security team needs to learn within hours which of the company's applications include it. What would have BEST prepared them?
opts: A larger firewall budget for the perimeter and internal segments
A software bill of materials for every application
Annual penetration tests of the network and external perimeter
A policy banning all open-source software from every project
why: An SBOM and composition analysis make it quick to identify where components are used. Firewalls and annual pen tests do not tell you which libraries are inside applications, and a ban on open source is unrealistic and does not remove existing use.

q: A company is buying a commercial application that will process customer data. What should be done BEFORE signing the contract?
opts: Assess the vendor's security practices and write security terms into the contract
Accept the vendor's claim that the product follows best practice and is secure
Plan to test security only after deployment into production, once users are on it
Rely on the product's popularity in the market as proof that it is secure
why: Responsibility is not transferred with the purchase, so due diligence and contractual security requirements must come first. Taking claims on trust, testing only after production deployment and relying on popularity all leave unmanaged risk.

q: An auditor finds database passwords hard-coded in application source code stored in a shared repository. What is the BEST remediation?
opts: Make the repository private but leave the passwords in the code and its history
Obfuscate the passwords with a simple encoding so they are not readable at a glance
Add a comment asking developers not to share the code outside the team
Move secrets to a vault, rotate the exposed credentials and scan for secrets
why: Exposed secrets must be treated as compromised and rotated, and a vault with runtime retrieval prevents recurrence. Restricting the repository leaves the secrets in history, encoding is not protection, and comments are not controls.

q: A team runs a build pipeline that deploys to production automatically. An attacker who obtains a developer's pipeline token could ship malicious code. Which control BEST reduces this risk?
opts: Protect pipeline credentials, require approvals and sign build artifacts
Make the pipeline run faster so deployments finish before an attacker can react
Store pipeline tokens in the source repository so the whole team can find them
Give every developer full administrator rights to the pipeline for flexibility
why: The pipeline is part of the attack surface, so controlling credentials, requiring review and approvals, and verifying signed artifacts limit what a stolen token can achieve. Speed is irrelevant, and wide privileges or stored tokens increase risk.

q: An Agile team delivers every two weeks. How should security BEST be integrated?
opts: Perform one large security review after the final sprint of the project
Defer security to a separate project after the product has launched
Rely only on the operations team to protect the application once it is in production
Add security criteria to stories, with automated security tests each sprint
why: Security must keep pace with iterations, through stories, acceptance criteria and automation. A single review at the end creates the same late discovery problem, and deferring or leaving it to operations leaves the code unprotected.

q: The vendor of a business-critical application the company uses is a small firm. The buyer worries about what happens if the vendor goes out of business. Which arrangement addresses this concern?
opts: A penetration test of the vendor's public website each year
Source code escrow with defined release conditions
A longer password policy for users of the application
A SOC 3 report from the vendor's auditor
why: Escrow places the source with a neutral party and releases it to the customer under agreed conditions, such as bankruptcy. A website pen test, password policy and SOC 3 report do not protect continued maintenance of the software.

q: During threat modeling of an order service, a team notes that an attacker could alter the price field in a request while it travels from the browser to the server. Which STRIDE category does this threat belong to?
opts: Spoofing, because the attacker pretends to be another user
Tampering, because the data is modified in transit
Repudiation, because the user could later deny placing the order
Elevation of privilege, because the attacker gains rights that were never granted
why: Changing data that the system relies on is tampering, a violation of integrity. Spoofing is impersonation, repudiation is denying an action when nothing proves otherwise, and elevation of privilege is gaining rights that were not granted; none describes modifying the price field.

q: Management asks how the organization can measure and improve its software security practices over time using a structured framework with prescriptive guidance. Which choice fits BEST?
opts: OWASP Software Assurance Maturity Model (SAMM)
A SOC 2 report issued for a service provider
A one-time penetration test of the application
A change advisory board for production changes
why: SAMM provides a prescriptive model to assess practices and plan improvements. A SOC 2 report is an attestation about a service, a pen test is a point-in-time technical test, and a change board manages changes.

q: Which two actions are part of secure input handling in a web application? (Choose two.)
opts: Validate input on the server using allow lists for expected format and length
Encode output for the context in which it is displayed
Rely on client-side JavaScript checks as the main protection
Block input only if it contains known attack strings
Accept any input and trust the database to reject bad data
why: Server-side allow-list validation and contextual output encoding are the core practices. Client-side checks are bypassable, block lists miss variants, and trusting the database is a late and unreliable defense.

q: Which two controls help protect the software supply chain? (Choose two.)
opts: Verify signatures and provenance of dependencies and build artifacts
Pin dependency versions and monitor them for known vulnerabilities
Automatically pull the newest unverified package version at every build
Allow developers to publish builds from personal laptops
Disable logging in the build system
why: Verification and pinned, monitored dependencies reduce the chance of tampered or vulnerable components. Pulling unverified newest versions, building on personal laptops and disabling logs all weaken integrity and visibility.

q: Which two statements about SAST and DAST are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: SAST analyzes code without running it and can point to the line of code involved
DAST tests a running application and can find runtime and configuration issues
DAST requires access to the application's source code
SAST can only be run after the application is deployed
SAST and DAST are identical and interchangeable
why: SAST examines code statically early in development, and DAST probes a running build. DAST does not require source, SAST does not require deployment, and they find different issue types.

q: A company is evaluating open-source components for a new product. Which two practices are appropriate? (Choose two.)
