opts: Maintain an inventory of components and versions, such as through an SBOM
Check licenses and known vulnerabilities before adopting a component
Assume widely used packages are always secure
Allow any developer to add dependencies with no review
Never update components after release
why: Inventory and pre-adoption checks give control over both vulnerability and licensing risk. Popularity does not imply security, uncontrolled additions create unknown risk, and stale components accumulate vulnerabilities.

q: Client-side input validation alone is sufficient to protect a web application from malformed or malicious input.
opts: True
False
why: Attackers can bypass the browser and send requests directly, so validation must be enforced on the server.

q: Fixing a security defect during the design phase generally costs less than fixing it after release.
opts: True
False
why: Cost rises as a defect moves through the life cycle, which is the reason for shifting security left.

q: A web application firewall is a replacement for fixing vulnerable code.
opts: True
False
why: A WAF is a compensating control that can provide virtual patching in the short term, but the underlying flaw should still be fixed.

q: Code signing proves that the software contains no malicious code.
opts: True
False
why: Signing proves who published the code and that it was not changed afterwards. A signed program can still be malicious, particularly if a signing key is stolen.

q: In the STRIDE model, repudiation refers to a user denying that they performed an action, countered by strong logging and non-repudiation controls.
opts: True
False
why: Repudiation threatens accountability, and logging, digital signatures and audit trails are the typical countermeasures.

q: DevSecOps aims to automate security checks into the delivery pipeline instead of treating security as a separate gate at the end.
opts: True
False
why: DevSecOps integrates scanning, testing and policy checks into the pipeline so feedback comes early and releases stay fast.

q: A project has unclear requirements and high technical risk. Management wants a model that repeats cycles of planning, risk analysis, engineering and evaluation. Which development model fits?
opts: The waterfall model, with all requirements fixed at the start
A single-pass big-bang release with testing at the end only
A maintenance-only model with no new development
The spiral model
why: The spiral model is built around repeated risk analysis in each cycle. Waterfall assumes stable requirements, a single big-bang release defers risk discovery and a maintenance-only model is not a development approach.

q: A Scrum team treats security work as something for the security department to do after the sprint. Defects found late delay releases. Which change BEST integrates security into the team's process?
opts: Skip sprint reviews to save time for security reviews
Move the security review to the final week of the project
Ask developers to avoid any security work during the sprint, so that features ship quickly and the security department can review the finished product later on
Add security stories and abuse cases to the backlog and include security checks in the definition of done
why: Making security work visible, estimated and part of done keeps it in every sprint. Skipping reviews, leaving security until the end and avoiding it entirely all produce the late discoveries the team is trying to avoid.

q: A company with 40 Agile teams adopts the Scaled Agile Framework and finds each team applying different security standards. Which action BEST addresses the inconsistency?
opts: Remove security requirements for any team smaller than ten people, because small teams are easy to supervise and rarely build high-risk features for customers
Run one annual security review for all teams after delivery
Define shared security requirements and automated pipeline checks, with security architects involved in release planning
Allow each team to define its own standards without coordination
why: At scale, common standards and automation applied through planning and the pipeline give consistency without blocking teams. Independent standards recreate the problem, size is not a risk exemption and annual reviews are too late.

q: A company wants to compare its software security program with what many real organizations actually do, rather than follow a prescribed roadmap. Which resource is the BEST fit?
opts: The CVSS specification, which scores the severity of vulnerabilities
BSIMM, which records observed practices across many software security programs
OWASP SAMM, a prescriptive roadmap of practices and maturity levels to adopt
The CWE list, which catalogs types of software weakness
why: BSIMM is descriptive: it reports what many real organizations do, which suits benchmarking. SAMM is the prescriptive roadmap, CWE is a catalog of weakness types and CVSS scores vulnerability severity.

q: A critical application reaches the end of its life and is switched off, but its database, service accounts and API keys remain. What does this show?
opts: Retirement was incomplete: data, accounts and keys should be disposed of or revoked as part of decommissioning
The application is secure because it is no longer running
The service accounts are harmless because nobody uses them
The keys should be kept indefinitely in a shared folder in case the application returns, since generating new ones would take extra effort for the team
why: Secure retirement removes or migrates data and revokes credentials, otherwise the leftovers become an attack path. A stopped application does not make leftover accounts and keys safe, and keeping keys indefinitely increases exposure.

q: A developer fixes a production bug by pushing code directly and bypassing review and testing because the change was small. A week later the change causes an outage. Which control would MOST likely have prevented this?
opts: More comments in the source code explaining each change, together with a short description in the commit message for every fix that is pushed
A longer password for the developer's account
Faster hardware for the production servers
Formal change management with separated environments and a required approval and test gate
why: Change management and separation of environments enforce review and testing before production. Comments, longer passwords and faster hardware do not prevent unreviewed changes.

q: Security staff are consulted only after the design is complete, and they identify problems that would require a redesign. Which organizational approach BEST fixes this?
opts: A policy that bans security staff from the design stage to avoid delays to the schedule
A contract clause that blames the developers for any flaws found after release
An integrated product team in which security participates from requirements onward
A separate review board that meets after release to look at what was built
why: An integrated product team gives security a seat from the start, reducing late surprises. Post-release boards, banning security from design and blame clauses do not find problems early.

q: A web application passes a user-supplied filename to a function that opens files from a directory. A tester retrieves a system password file by supplying a name with repeated "../" sequences. What is the BEST fix?
opts: Encrypt the web server's network connection with TLS
Canonicalize the path, restrict access to an allowed base directory and run with least privilege
Hide the directory name from users, so that attackers cannot guess where the application keeps its files and which paths are worth trying
Add a banner that warns against reading other files
why: Path traversal is stopped by resolving the real path, confining access to a base directory and limiting process rights. Hiding names, banners and TLS do not stop the application from opening the file.

q: An application accepts serialized objects from clients and deserializes them with a native mechanism that can create arbitrary classes. Which risk is MOST significant?
opts: Remote code execution through crafted objects
Loss of audit logs because of network latency
Weaker TLS cipher selection
Slow page rendering for mobile users
why: Untrusted serialized data can instantiate classes that execute code during deserialization. Audit logs, cipher selection and rendering speed are not the central risk of this design.

q: A document service checks a user's permission when the document list is first loaded and then serves later requests for the same document without checking again, even after that user's access has been revoked. Which secure design principle is violated?
opts: Fail secure: when a check cannot be completed or errors, access is denied
Defense in depth: several independent layers of protection stand between attacker and asset
Least privilege: each user is given only the rights needed for the task
Complete mediation: every access to every object is checked against current authorization
why: Complete mediation requires every access to be checked against current authorization, so a cached or one-time decision lets a revoked user keep reading. Fail secure concerns what happens when a check errors, defense in depth adds layers and least privilege limits the rights granted; none of them describes skipping later checks.

q: A user changes the order number in a URL from 1001 to 1002 and sees another customer's order. Which vulnerability class is this, and what is the FIX?
opts: SQL injection; use stored procedures only
Buffer overflow; use a larger buffer
Broken access control; enforce server-side authorization on each object request
Cross-site scripting; encode all output and add a content security policy so that the browser blocks any script injected into the order page
why: Accessing another user's object by changing an identifier is broken access control (insecure direct object reference), fixed by checking ownership on the server. XSS, SQL injection and buffer overflow have different causes and fixes.

q: An API returns complete customer records to any caller that supplies a valid token, and the client application hides fields the user should not see. Which control BEST fixes the weakness?
opts: Increase the length of the API token and shorten its lifetime, so that a caller needs to authenticate more often to retrieve complete records
Rename the API endpoints so they are harder to guess
Enforce authorization on the server for each object and property, returning only permitted fields
Hide the fields in the mobile user interface more thoroughly
why: Authorization must be enforced by the server for each object and field, since client-side hiding is bypassed easily. A longer token or renamed endpoints do not stop an authenticated caller from reading everything.

q: A GraphQL API in production allows unlimited query depth and exposes its full schema to unauthenticated callers. Which response is BEST?
opts: Remove authentication for the schema so it is easier to document
Disable introspection in production and limit query depth and cost, alongside authorization checks
Allow unlimited depth because GraphQL is efficient, and rely on the clients to send only reasonable queries that do not overload the service
Expose more of the schema so that developers can integrate quickly
why: Limiting depth and cost prevents resource abuse, disabling introspection reduces reconnaissance and authorization protects data. The other options expand exposure or remove protections.

q: A company is picking a language for a new network-facing service that parses untrusted input at high speed. Which choice BEST reduces memory-corruption vulnerabilities?
opts: A memory-safe language such as Rust or Go, with standard libraries for parsing
C with manual memory management and no compiler hardening, because it produces the smallest and fastest code for parsing untrusted input at line speed
Assembly language, for the best control of memory
Any language, because the choice has no security effect
why: Memory-safe languages remove most buffer and use-after-free flaws. C without hardening and assembly leave memory management to the developer, and the claim that language has no effect ignores a major source of vulnerabilities.

q: A developer plans to implement a custom encryption routine for a new application because the standard library is "too slow." What is the BEST guidance?
opts: Approve the routine if the developer is experienced
Keep the algorithm secret so attackers cannot study it
Use a shorter key and fewer rounds to improve speed, since the routine is custom and attackers are unlikely to study an unusual algorithm
Use the vetted library with appropriate algorithms and tune the design, rather than writing custom cryptography
why: Cryptography should come from vetted libraries, since subtle mistakes in custom code are common. Experience does not substitute for review, secrecy of the algorithm is not a control and shorter keys weaken protection.

q: An attacker compromises a company's build server and inserts a backdoor into software that is then signed with the company's own key. Which control would have MOST reduced this risk?
opts: More colorful dashboards for the development team
Allowing every developer to administer the build server
Hardened, ephemeral build agents with scoped credentials, provenance and reproducible builds
A longer software license agreement with stronger warranty language and a clause that requires customers to report any problem within a month
why: Protecting the build environment and verifying provenance makes tampering hard and detectable. License text, dashboards and broad administrator rights do not protect the build.

q: A repository holds the source for the company's flagship product. Any developer can push to the main branch without review, and a leaked pipeline token was found in a public paste. Which combination is the BEST response?
opts: Give the intern a copy of the token for testing
Require protected branches with reviews, SSO with MFA, secret scanning, and rotate the leaked token
Keep the token in place and monitor for abuse, since rotating it would require changes to every pipeline and could interrupt several releases
Make the repository public to improve transparency
why: Protected branches, strong authentication and secret scanning address the weaknesses, and a leaked token must be rotated at once. Keeping it, publishing the repository or sharing the token increases exposure.

q: An auditor asks how the company can prove that a specific production change was reviewed and approved. Which evidence is BEST?
opts: A commit linked to an approved change ticket with a recorded review and a deployment log
A verbal statement from the developer, confirmed by their manager in a short meeting, that the change was reviewed and approved before release
A screenshot of the developer's desktop
The final state of the source code with no history
why: Linked tickets, reviews and deployment logs show who did what and who approved it. Statements, screenshots and a code snapshot without history do not provide verifiable traceability.

q: A product owner measures software security only by the number of scans run each month. Which metric would be MORE meaningful?
opts: The number of security meetings held each month, since a regular cadence of meetings shows that the program is taken seriously by the teams
The number of pages in the secure coding policy
The number of developers who attended any training
Flaws found after release and the time taken to fix them, tracked by severity
why: Escaped flaws and time to fix are outcome measures of effectiveness. Meetings, policy length and attendance are activity measures that do not show whether software is more secure.

q: A company buys a commercial application. The vendor provides a SOC 2 report but refuses to commit to patch timelines or breach notification. What is the BEST next step?
opts: Sign and add the terms later after problems arise
Skip any security review because the vendor is well known
Negotiate security terms into the contract, such as patch timelines, notification and audit rights, before signing
Sign the contract, since the SOC 2 report is enough to show that the vendor takes security seriously, and revisit the topic at renewal
why: Security obligations should be contractual before purchase, when the buyer has leverage. A SOC 2 report does not replace commitments, adding terms later is hard and reputation is not assurance.

q: A company uses a SaaS enterprise application and has added custom scripts and connectors that expose customer data to an external partner. Who is MOST responsible for the security of those customizations?
opts: No one, because SaaS is secured by default
The customer, because customizations and integrations are the customer's responsibility even in SaaS
The SaaS provider, because it hosts the platform and operates the infrastructure that the custom scripts and connectors are running on top of
The partner receiving the data, because they asked for it
why: Under shared responsibility the customer owns its configuration, identities, data and custom code. The provider secures the platform, the partner is a recipient and nobody is not an option.

q: A development team uses an AI coding assistant that suggests a package name the team has never heard of. Which action is MOST appropriate?
opts: Disable all scanning to avoid false positives
Verify the package in a trusted registry, review its maintenance and vulnerabilities, and scan it before use
Install it immediately because the suggestion came from an AI tool that has seen millions of repositories and usually names well-known packages
Install it only on a production server to see if it works
why: AI suggestions are untrusted and may name non-existent or malicious packages, so verification and scanning are needed. Immediate installation, testing in production and disabling scanning each increase risk.

q: A chatbot connected to internal documents and an email-sending tool follows instructions hidden in a web page that a user asked it to summarize, and mails out confidential files. Which design change BEST reduces this risk?
opts: Limit the model's permissions, treat retrieved content as untrusted and require human approval for sensitive actions
Make the model's system prompt longer and more polite, and tell it clearly never to follow instructions that appear inside retrieved web pages
Give the model administrator access so it can resolve conflicts
Disable logging so that sensitive data is not recorded
why: Prompt injection is mitigated by limiting what the model can do, separating untrusted content and requiring approval for impactful actions. A longer prompt does not prevent override, administrator access increases impact and disabling logs removes visibility.

q: The spiral model places risk analysis at the center of each development cycle.
opts: True
False
why: Each loop of the spiral includes planning, risk analysis, engineering and evaluation, which is why it suits projects with uncertain requirements and high risk.

q: OWASP SAMM is a descriptive model that only reports what other organizations do, while BSIMM is a prescriptive roadmap.
opts: True
False
why: It is the other way round: SAMM is prescriptive (a roadmap with maturity levels), and BSIMM is descriptive (observations of real programs).

q: Open-source software is secure by default because many people can read the code.
opts: True
False
why: Visibility does not guarantee review or maintenance. Open-source components must still be inventoried, assessed and patched.

q: The NIST SSDF organizes practices into four groups: Prepare the Organization, Protect the Software, Produce Well-Secured Software and Respond to Vulnerabilities.
opts: True
False
why: These four groups (PO, PS, PW and RV) make up SP 800-218.

q: A secure application should fail closed, denying access when an authorization check errors.
opts: True
False
why: Failing secure prevents an error from becoming a bypass; detailed errors are logged on the server and not shown to users.

q: Which TWO practices help secure a code repository? (Choose two.)
opts: Allow all developers to commit directly to the main branch without review
Enable secret scanning and rotate any exposed credential
Store pipeline tokens in the repository for convenience
Make internal repositories public to increase collaboration
Require reviews and passing checks before merging to protected branches
why: Protected branches with review and secret scanning with rotation reduce unreviewed changes and credential exposure. Direct commits, stored tokens and public exposure weaken security.

q: Which TWO terms should a customer seek in a contract for acquired software? (Choose two.)
opts: A clause allowing the vendor to change security practices without notice
A ban on the customer scanning its own deployment
Patch and vulnerability notification timelines
A promise that no vulnerabilities will ever occur
Rights to review security assessments or audit
why: Timelines and review rights make security enforceable. A zero-vulnerability promise is not realistic, and the other clauses remove customer oversight.

q: Which TWO are good safeguards for an API exposed to the internet? (Choose two.)
opts: Authorize each request on the server at the object and function level
Rely on obscure endpoint names for protection
Apply rate limits and size limits to prevent resource exhaustion
Return detailed stack traces to help client developers debug
Keep old API versions running without monitoring
why: Per-request authorization and rate limits address the top API risks. Obscurity, verbose errors and unmonitored old versions create exposure.
